math.context: If 34x + 37 = 1227, what is x?

why.A: Subtract 37, then divide by 34: x = 35.

why.C: Substitution gives 1261, not 1227.

reading.context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: a repair that changes what an object is able to say.
a craftsman teaching an apprentice to service a mechanism.
a family disagreement about the value of an inherited object.
the closure of a rural railway line and its local effects.

why.A: Correct. Mira arrives intending to erase the scratch and leaves able to read it; the mechanism is fixed and the mark is kept.
why.B: The grandfather does service the mechanism, but that hour is the setting for the point, not the point. Mira learns nothing about oiling pivots.
why.C: Nobody argues. Mira offers to repaint, is told what the mark means, and changes her own mind without being opposed.
why.D: The closed line is one clause of background. The passage is about the face of the clock, not the fate of the railway.

reading.context: According to the passage, the grandfather replaces:

choices.text: the scratched face of the clock with a new one.
a suspension spring that had become brittle.
the two pivots that he had previously oiled.
the wooden case, which had warped out of true.

why.A: He deliberately leaves the face alone. Replacing it is what Mira wanted and what the passage is about him not doing.
why.B: Correct. He puts in "a new suspension spring in place of one that had gone brittle" — the only thing replaced rather than cleaned.
why.C: The pivots are oiled, not replaced. The passage lists the two actions separately in the same sentence.
why.D: He turns the case over to open the back. Nothing in the passage says the case is damaged or worked on.

reading.context: It can reasonably be inferred that the grandfather spends the first hour on the mechanism because he:

choices.text: wants Mira to lose interest in repainting the face.
has not yet noticed the long scratch on the clock face.
thinks the clock working matters more than the clock looking new.
is waiting for better light before starting the more delicate work.

why.A: He answers her offer directly with a question about the mark. Nothing suggests he is stalling her.
why.B: He turns the case over and asks her what made the scratch, so he has plainly seen it.
why.C: Correct. Offered a cosmetic job, he opens the back instead and works only on what makes it run.
why.D: Light is never mentioned. The hour is spent on specific repairs the passage lists.

reading.context: As it is used in the final paragraph, the word "legible" most nearly means:

choices.text: neatly written in a careful hand.
able to be read for its meaning.
large enough to be seen clearly.
permanent, and no longer removable.

why.A: Handwriting is the everyday sense of the word and the wrong one here. The mark was scored into metal, not written.
why.B: Correct. The sentence sets it against "prettier": the mark did not improve in looks, it became something Mira could read a history off.
why.C: Size is not at issue. Mira could see the scratch perfectly well on the walk to the workshop.
why.D: She could still repaint it and says so. The change is in what it means to her, not in whether it can be removed.

reading.context: The last sentence of the passage mainly serves to:

choices.text: state the trade Mira has accepted and her judgement of it.
raise a doubt about whether the repair was worth the effort.
explain the mechanical reason the clock keeps poor time.
return to the workshop scene described in the second paragraph.

why.A: Correct. It names both halves — keeps time badly, says something exactly — and reports that she prefers this arrangement.
why.B: It does the opposite. She states a preference for the outcome she has.
why.C: No mechanical cause is given. The clock is simply described as keeping time badly.
why.D: The sentence is set at home, on a shelf, after the workshop scene has ended.

reading.context: The author's attitude toward the borrowing statistic is best described as:

choices.text: openly hostile to the people who chose to use it.
critical of its fit to this case, not of the measure itself.
indifferent, since the branch stayed open in the end.
admiring of its precision by comparison with the door counter.

why.A: Nobody is blamed. The recommendation is even called uncontested, which is reported rather than condemned.
why.B: Correct. The passage calls it "a reasonable proxy" for one kind of branch and "close to useless" for the other.
why.C: The passage spends its length explaining why the measure misled, which is not indifference to it.
why.D: The door counter is the instrument that settled the matter. The borrowing figure is the one that failed.

reading.context: Which detail most directly supports the claim that the branch was being measured wrongly?

choices.text: It was the weakest of eleven branches on the chosen measure.
The closure was recommended in 2011 and not seriously contested.
Its late-afternoon visitors read in the building and rarely borrowed.
A volunteer group compiled door-counter figures across a full school term.

why.A: This is the measure producing its result. It is the finding in dispute, not evidence about whether the finding is sound.
why.B: The date and the lack of objection describe how the decision was taken, not whether the instrument fitted.
why.C: Correct. A metric that counts departures misses a population that stays, and this names that population.
why.D: This is how the correction was delivered. What made the original wrong is the behaviour of the visitors.

reading.context: The passage is organised as:

choices.text: a decision, the evidence it missed, and how it was reversed.
a chronological history of eleven branches in one district.
a comparison of two libraries that have opposite funding models.
an argument for closing branches that lend very few books.

why.A: Correct. Paragraph one gives the closure, two and three give what the metric could not see, four gives the reversal.
why.B: Only one branch is followed. The other ten appear in a single clause as a ranking.
why.C: A second library is never described. The comparison in the passage is between two kinds of visitor.
why.D: The passage works against that conclusion, showing the lending figure to be the wrong test here.

reading.context: The passage distinguishes the two groups of library users principally by whether they:

choices.text: are children or adults with daytime employment.
arrive before or after half past four in the afternoon.
take something away or remain inside the building.
use the printed collection or the public terminals.

why.A: Age describes the afternoon crowd but is not the distinction the argument turns on; the statistic cannot see age either.
why.B: The time marks when the second group arrives. It is a symptom of the split, not what makes the measure fail.
why.C: Correct. The passage states it directly: a borrowing statistic counts departures, so a branch whose visitors stay reads as empty.
why.D: Terminals are one of several things the second group does. Some of them are reading printed books in the building.

reading.context: In saying that the two populations "look identical on the spreadsheet", the author means that:

choices.text: the two groups contain roughly the same number of people.
the records kept for the branch were careless over many years.
the council had merged the figures for all eleven branches.
the recorded figure is the same whichever group produced it.

why.A: No count of either group is given, and the sentence is about what the figure registers rather than how many people there are.
why.B: The figures are accurate. The complaint is about what they measure, not about how carefully they were taken.
why.C: Each branch is ranked separately — that ranking is how this one came last.
why.D: Correct. A visitor who borrows nothing and a visitor who was never there both register as zero issues.

reading.context: The main point of the passage is that acoustic monitoring:

choices.text: has replaced walked transects in nearly all marsh surveys.
fails in wind and is therefore unsuited to coastal work.
has limits that are specifiable, which is its real advantage.
counts rails more accurately than any other available method.

why.A: No claim about adoption is made. The passage compares the two methods without saying which is more used.
why.B: Wind is one stated limit among three, and the closing paragraph explicitly declines that conclusion.
why.C: Correct. The last paragraph makes it the point: wrong in ways that can be written down is a more useful property.
why.D: The passage says the opposite — it measures activity, not abundance, and cannot count individuals.

reading.context: The passage identifies which of the following as a limit of acoustic monitoring?

choices.text: It cannot distinguish one species of rail from another.
It requires an observer to remain present before dawn.
It reports activity rather than a count of individuals.
It works only during the hours immediately after sunrise.

why.A: The passage says the reverse: each species keeps to a narrow, repetitive call, which is why rails suit the method.
why.B: The recorder is fixed before dawn and collected days later. Leaving the observer out is the method’s whole premise.
why.C: Correct. It cannot separate one bird calling ten times from ten calling once, so it measures activity, not abundance.
why.D: No restriction to particular hours is given. The recorder runs unattended across days.

reading.context: The passage suggests that a researcher who needed the number of rails in a marsh would:

choices.text: find the recordings alone insufficient for that question.
prefer acoustic monitoring for its freedom from observer error.
be unable to survey the marsh by any method now available.
need to place recorders at a radius wider than the marsh itself.

why.A: Correct. Activity is not abundance, and the passage states the method cannot tell ten calls from ten birds.
why.B: Freedom from the flushing problem is real, but it does not supply a count, which is what this researcher needs.
why.C: The walked transect is still described as available; it is characterised as having different errors, not as unusable.
why.D: Radius limits what the recorder hears. Widening it past the marsh would not solve the one-bird-or-ten problem.

reading.context: As it is used in the third paragraph, "precise" most nearly means:

choices.text: narrow enough that they are of no practical concern.
measured to several decimal places of accuracy.
strict, in the sense of harshly limiting.
specific, and therefore able to be stated exactly.

why.A: The limits matter a great deal — one of them rules out quiet species entirely in wind.
why.B: Decimal accuracy is the numerical sense of the word. The paragraph then lists limits, not measurements.
why.C: Severity is not the contrast. The sentence sets "precise" against "vague", not against "mild".
why.D: Correct. The sentence opposes precise to vague, and what follows is three limits each stated exactly.

reading.context: The first paragraph functions primarily to:

choices.text: establish the problem the second paragraph answers.
argue that rails are the hardest marsh bird to survey.
describe the equipment used in a walked transect.
summarise the findings of a completed marsh survey.

why.A: Correct. It states the flaw in walking a marsh, and the next paragraph opens by saying acoustic monitoring avoids both errors.
why.B: Rails are called easier to hear than to see, which is a fact about method, not a ranking of difficulty among species.
why.C: No equipment appears. The paragraph describes what happens to the birds when a person walks through.
why.D: No survey results are reported anywhere in the passage.

reading.context: The author's attitude toward Hollar's blank spaces is one of:

choices.text: reluctance to judge a practice so far removed in time.
considered approval of a choice his contemporaries misread.
amusement at a mapmaker who could not finish his commission.
concern that the chart misled the admiralty that paid for it.

why.A: The passage judges plainly, calling the choice deliberate rather than lazy and the later verdict kinder and correct.
why.B: Correct. It argues the blankness was principled and that two centuries have been right to admire it.
why.C: It argues against the unfinished reading, using the notebooks to show the gaps were intended.
why.D: Less useful to the admiralty is conceded in passing and immediately outweighed by the use to later surveyors.

reading.context: Which evidence does the author use to show Hollar's blanks were intentional?

choices.text: The chart is still admired by cartographic historians today.
A fifth of the chart’s surface carries no detail of any kind.
His notebooks record a refusal to draw a coast he had not seen.
The conventions of the period called for a cartouche or wind rose.

why.A: Later admiration is the passage’s conclusion. It shows how the chart was received, not what Hollar meant by it.
why.B: The extent of the blankness is the thing to be explained. On its own it fits the unfinished reading just as well.
why.C: Correct. The notebooks state the reason in his own words, which is what turns an absence into a decision.
why.D: The convention establishes what he departed from. It is the background against which the choice stands out.

reading.context: The passage moves from:

choices.text: a modern verdict, to the reasoning behind it, to its consequences.
a biography of Hollar, to his methods, to his later reputation.
a technical problem, to two solutions, to a choice made between them.
a general rule about charts, to an exception, to a restatement.

why.A: Correct. It opens on what is admired today, turns to the notebooks for why, and closes on who the chart served.
why.B: Hollar’s life is absent. Only one chart and one notebook entry appear.
why.C: Two solutions are never weighed. The ornamental convention is described as what he declined, not as a live option.
why.D: The convention is stated to be departed from, and the passage does not return to endorse it.

reading.context: The passage contrasts a sea monster with an invented headland chiefly on the grounds that:

choices.text: one was cheaper for an engraver to cut than the other.
one would be taken as decoration and the other as fact.
one was fashionable in 1732 and the other had fallen out of use.
one occupied more of the chart’s surface than the other.

why.A: Cost is never raised. The distinction the passage draws is about how each mark would be read.
why.B: Correct. The passage says it almost in those words: a monster is understood as ornament, a headland as a headland.
why.C: Both belong to the same conventional repertoire of the period; neither is described as out of fashion.
why.D: Size is not the issue. A small invented headland would carry the same false claim.

reading.context: The statement that two centuries "have been kinder to it than its first readers were" conveys that:

choices.text: the physical chart has survived in unusually good condition.
early copies were damaged and later reproductions were not.
later judgement has valued precisely what first readers disliked.
the chart was forgotten for a long period and later rediscovered.

why.A: Physical survival is never mentioned, and the clause is immediately glossed by a reason about how it was judged.
why.B: No copies or reproductions appear in the passage at all.
why.C: Correct. The sentence finishes "for exactly the reason they disliked it", making the reversal the whole point.
why.D: Nothing suggests neglect. The contrast is between two verdicts, not between obscurity and fame.

reading.context: The passage is best described as an account of:

choices.text: a practice whose purpose becomes clear only through doing it.
a disagreement between a student and the leader of her group.
a musician deciding to found an ensemble of her own.
a technique for correcting rhythm that a teacher hands on.

why.A: Correct. Devi misreads the rule for two weeks, learns what it does by sitting through it, and later refuses to explain it in advance.
why.B: There is no disagreement. Devi waits politely, then finds the exercise works.
why.C: Her own group appears in one clause, years later, as evidence that she kept the rule.
why.D: No teacher passes on a technique; the passage stresses that no teacher had ever mentioned her rushing.

reading.context: According to the passage, during the ten-minute rule the players:

choices.text: listen to a recording without commenting on it.
warm up quietly before the full rehearsal begins.
take turns describing what went wrong last week.
play through the previous week’s material once.

why.A: Correct. The passage states both halves: they hear the previous week’s recording, and no comment is allowed during it.
why.B: Devi assumed it was a warm-up. The passage introduces that reading in order to correct it.
why.C: Comment is explicitly forbidden while the recording runs.
why.D: Nobody plays for the first ten minutes — that is the rule itself.

reading.context: It can be inferred that Devi had not noticed her rushing earlier because she:

choices.text: had been taught by someone who valued speed in performance.
could not hear her own playing while she was producing it.
had joined the Thursday group only two weeks previously.
played too quietly for the fault to be audible to others.

why.A: Her teachers are mentioned only to say none of them raised it. No teaching philosophy is described.
why.B: Correct. Ravi states the principle and Devi’s experience confirms it — obvious at once when she was not playing.
why.C: She is at the rehearsal from the first paragraph; the delay was in hearing herself, not in arriving.
why.D: Volume is never mentioned, and others hearing her is not what changed.

reading.context: As it is used in the fourth paragraph, "cost her no effort" most nearly means that she:

choices.text: was given help by the other five members of the group.
found the passage easier than the ones around it.
had been practising the correction outside rehearsal.
stopped doing it without having to try to stop.

why.A: The others never comment; the rule forbids it during the recording and no coaching is described.
why.B: No particular passage of music is singled out as easy or hard anywhere in the paragraph.
why.C: Outside practice is not mentioned, and it would contradict the claim that no effort was involved.
why.D: Correct. The next clause spells it out: she had simply stopped being able to do it.

reading.context: The final paragraph contributes to the passage mainly by:

choices.text: showing that the rule outlasted the group it began in.
revealing that Devi eventually abandoned the practice.
explaining the mechanical cause of a rhythmic fault.
identifying the week in which most players improve.

why.A: Correct. Devi carries the rule to a group of her own years later, which is what turns one rehearsal into a practice.
why.B: She keeps it. What she declines to do is explain it in advance.
why.C: No cause for the rushing is offered anywhere; the passage is about noticing it.
why.D: Week three is when people work the rule out, which is about the rule, not about improvement.

reading.context: The passage is primarily about:

choices.text: a comparison that turned out to vary more than one thing.
the correct watering schedule for beans grown indoors.
a teacher correcting two classes that kept poor records.
the advantages of germinating seeds beside a bright window.

why.A: Correct. The closing paragraph says it outright: they ran a test of two levels of attention, not of two watering schedules.
why.B: No schedule is endorsed. The whole point is that the result cannot be read as being about watering at all.
why.C: The records were good enough to find the problem in — the notebook is where the extra actions were discovered.
why.D: Both classes used the same window, so light is held constant and cannot be what the passage is about.

reading.context: The notebook shows that, besides watering, the second class also:

choices.text: changed the variety of bean partway through the fortnight.
moved one tray away from a sill that had grown cold.
added fertiliser to the trays that were slowest to sprout.
watered its trays more often than the first class did.

why.A: Both classes planted the same variety, stated in the opening sentence as one of the things held constant.
why.B: Correct. The notebook lists it among the incidental actions: once moved a tray off a cold sill.
why.C: No fertiliser appears anywhere. The soil came from the same bag for both classes.
why.D: Frequency of watering is never compared. What differed was what triggered it, and what else happened alongside.

reading.context: The passage implies that the second class looked at its trays twice a day because:

choices.text: the teacher had instructed them to record daily observations.
their trays were germinating faster and needed closer watching.
their method required a judgement about whether soil was dry.
they suspected the first class of watering on the wrong days.

why.A: The teacher enters only afterwards, to ask what else had differed. No instruction to observe is described.
why.B: The faster germination is the result being explained. It cannot also be the reason they were looking.
why.C: Correct. Watering only when the surface looked dry means somebody has to go and look, which is stated directly.
why.D: No rivalry appears. The two classes are simply running different procedures.

reading.context: As it is used in the final paragraph, "consequences" most nearly means:

choices.text: penalties that followed from a mistake in procedure.
results that followed from adopting that method.
matters of serious importance to the experiment.
conclusions the class drew from their own results.

why.A: Nothing is being punished. The extra actions helped the plants; they simply were not the variable under test.
why.B: Correct. The sentence says the actions were not the method and were things the method brought about.
why.C: Importance is the other everyday sense of the word, and the sentence is about what caused the actions.
why.D: The class draws its conclusion later, after the teacher asks. These are actions, not conclusions.

reading.context: The second paragraph serves mainly to:

choices.text: state the result and the reading the rest of the passage tests.
describe the equipment the two classes had been given.
introduce the teacher who will later question the class.
list the variables the two classes had deliberately held constant.

why.A: Correct. It gives the three-day difference and calls the watering explanation the obvious reading, which the passage then undoes.
why.B: Equipment is covered in the first paragraph — trays, soil, window — not the second.
why.C: The teacher appears at the start of the third paragraph, not in this one.
why.D: The constants are in the opening sentence. This paragraph reports an outcome.

reading.context: The author's attitude toward the vendors is best described as:

choices.text: sympathetic to complaints that were accurate but incomplete.
impatient with traders unwilling to adapt to a better site.
sceptical that their reported fall in takings really occurred.
approving of a decision that improved the market in every way.

why.A: Correct. The passage grants that the square had every fault they named, and the closing line treats the miss as understandable.
why.B: The vendors wanted the move and got it. Nothing suggests they resisted change.
why.C: The fall is reported as fact — about a fifth within two months — with no doubt attached.
why.D: The move solved three problems and cost the market its passing trade, which the passage does not call an improvement overall.

reading.context: Which finding best supports the explanation the passage gives for the fall in takings?

choices.text: Shoppers interviewed afterwards said they liked the new space.
Deliveries to the old square had to be carried the last stretch.
The vendors who pushed for the move noticed the drop first.
Much of the old custom had been passing rather than intending.

why.A: Liking the site is what rules out the obvious explanation. It clears the ground without supplying the cause.
why.B: The delivery problem is one of the faults that justified moving, and it has nothing to do with attendance.
why.C: Who noticed first tells us about the vendors, not about why the shoppers stopped coming.
why.D: Correct. If most custom was incidental to the walk, moving off that walk removes it without any fault in the new site.

reading.context: The passage is built as:

choices.text: a decision with sound reasons, an unexpected result, and its cause.
a chronological history of one town centre over several decades.
two competing proposals, each with its own supporters and opponents.
a general claim about markets illustrated by four different towns.

why.A: Correct. Paragraph one gives the reasons, two the fall in takings, three and four what actually caused it.
why.B: Only one move is covered, over about two months. No longer history is given.
why.C: No alternative proposal is ever described; the square and the new site are before and after, not rivals.
why.D: One town is discussed throughout, and no general claim is stated before the example.

reading.context: The passage contrasts the two sites chiefly in terms of whether the market was:

choices.text: able to accommodate deliveries made by vehicle.
encountered on the way somewhere or travelled to.
pleasant to walk through on a busy Saturday morning.
supported by the vendors who traded there regularly.

why.A: Deliveries improved at the new site and had no bearing on whether shoppers arrived.
why.B: Correct. The passage names it directly: the market became a destination, and a destination has to be chosen.
why.C: Comfort improved with the move, which makes it the wrong axis for explaining a fall.
why.D: The vendors supported both the move and the market; their view did not change between sites.

reading.context: The final sentence — that the vendors identified every fault "except the one that was paying them" — works by:

choices.text: treating an advantage of the old site as though it were a defect.
suggesting the vendors had been dishonest about their own takings.
implying the town council had misled the vendors about the move.
claiming the new site had a fault the vendors had failed to see.

why.A: Correct. Cramped aisles on a busy walking route were the same fact as the passing trade, so the complaint and the income shared a cause.
why.B: The takings are reported straightforwardly. Nothing in the passage questions the vendors’ honesty.
why.C: The council is never described as promising anything, and the move delivered what it was meant to.
why.D: The interviews found nothing wrong with the new site. The missed item belonged to the old one.

reading.context: The central claim of the passage is that a translation should be judged by:

choices.text: how closely its rhyme scheme follows the original poem.
the number of images it manages to keep in position.
what it decided to give up, rather than by a ranking.
how naturally it reads to someone in the new language.

why.A: Rhyme is one of three things that can be kept, and the version that kept it paid for it by moving an image.
why.B: Counting preserved images would be another ranking, which is the approach Leena abandons partway through.
why.C: Correct. She stops ranking and instead writes, under each version, what that version chose to lose.
why.D: The version that read most beautifully is also the one that dropped a clause, so fluency alone settles nothing.

reading.context: According to the passage, the third translation:

choices.text: moved a lantern from the second line to the sixth.
preserved every image but allowed the metre to go slack.
omitted a clause that referred to the cold.
was the one Leena ranked first in the margin.

why.A: The lantern was moved by the first translation, which did it in order to keep the rhyme scheme.
why.B: Preserving the images and losing the metre describes the second version, not the third.
why.C: Correct. The third read beautifully in English and had quietly dropped a whole clause about the cold.
why.D: Her abandoned ranking read "1, 3, 2", which places the third second rather than first.

reading.context: Leena stops writing her ranking because she realises that the three versions:

choices.text: were produced by translators of very unequal skill.
were not all attempting to do the same thing.
contained errors she was not qualified to judge.
had been printed from the same faulty source text.

why.A: Skill is never raised. Each version is described as competently doing something different.
why.B: Correct. The passage states it: the ranking assumed the three were attempts at the same task, and they plainly were not.
why.C: She goes on to write three confident sentences about them, so lack of standing is not the problem.
why.D: One original poem is implied throughout, and nothing suggests a defective source.

reading.context: As it is used in the third paragraph, "spends" most nearly means:

choices.text: exhausts through careless and repeated overuse.
gives up one thing in order to obtain another.
passes a period of time working on something.
distributes evenly across several competing aims.

why.A: Carelessness is the opposite of the passage’s account; each loss is described as a judgement.
why.B: Correct. The clause finishes "to buy another", which makes the word a trade rather than a waste.
why.C: Time is the other common sense of the verb, and the sentence is about what the translator gives up.
why.D: Even distribution is precisely what the passage says is impossible — all three cannot be kept together.

reading.context: The final paragraph functions to:

choices.text: concede that the ranking she abandoned was right after all.
identify which of the three translations she finally preferred.
show what the alternative to ranking produced for her.
explain why the poem is difficult to translate into English.

why.A: She never returns to the ranking, and what replaces it is offered as the better instrument.
why.B: No preference is stated. The three sentences describe losses rather than crown a winner.
why.C: Correct. Three sentences naming what each gave up told her more about the original than the translations had.
why.D: Difficulty is established in the third paragraph as a general claim about translation, not here.

reading.context: The passage is mainly about Arun learning that:

choices.text: choosing what to leave out can be the harder skill.
his sister builds better model bridges than he does.
wooden kits contain more pieces than are supplied.
a bridge should always be tested before it is glued.

why.A: Correct. The second bridge uses two thirds of the wood, and the hour spent deciding where the rest would not go is called harder.
why.B: His sister supplies the drawing sheet and one remark. Her own bridge is never compared to his.
why.C: The kit has a fixed contents, and the point is that he need not use all of it.
why.D: Both bridges are tested after building. No testing sequence is recommended anywhere.

reading.context: The first bridge fails the third test by:

choices.text: breaking suddenly across the middle of the span.
tipping to one side as the weight was lowered on.
sagging in a way that did not reverse afterwards.
pulling apart at the glued joints near each end.

why.A: The passage is explicit that it did not break, and uses that to set up the slower kind of failure.
why.B: No sideways movement is described; the deformation is downward, in the middle.
why.C: Correct. It sagged slowly in the middle and the sag did not go away when the weight came off.
why.D: Joints and glue appear only in the account of the second bridge, which used less of both.

reading.context: It can be inferred that the drawing sheet was useful to Arun mainly because it:

choices.text: listed every piece the kit was supposed to contain.
gave measurements he had previously had to estimate.
showed a design rather stronger than the one he had chosen.
showed where the load travelled in three different spans.

why.A: A parts list would not have told him which pieces to leave out, which is the lesson he takes from it.
why.B: No measurement problem is described. His first bridge failed from where material sat, not from its size.
why.C: It shows three spans rather than one better one, and he goes on to design his own rather than copy any of them.
why.D: Correct. The sheet drew the same span three ways with a note under each about where the load went.

reading.context: As it is used in the first paragraph, "convincing" most nearly means:

choices.text: persuasive in argument to a sceptical listener.
looking as though it would do what it was for.
built precisely to the tolerances in the drawing.
heavy enough to remain stable under its own weight.

why.A: No argument is taking place. The word describes how the object struck Arun when he looked at it.
why.B: Correct. The clause pairs it with "looked", and the bridge then fails, so the look was not the performance.
why.C: He had not unfolded the drawing at that stage, so he could not have been building to it.
why.D: Weight is mentioned separately in the same sentence, which makes it a different property from this one.

reading.context: The single-sentence final paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.text: confirm the second approach worked, with room to spare.
suggest that his sister had exaggerated the test weights.
return the passage to the sagging of the first bridge.
introduce a competition the two of them plan to enter.

why.A: Correct. It clears every weight in the box, and the last one is marked out as beyond what anyone had held.
why.B: Her remark raises the bar rather than lowering it, and the bridge then meets it.
why.C: The first bridge is finished with by the third paragraph and is not mentioned again.
why.D: No competition appears anywhere in the passage.

reading.context: The author's attitude toward the pupil's conclusion is:

choices.text: dismissive of a pupil who had not done the reading.
undecided, since the shade readings were inconclusive.
corrective, while treating the error as understandable.
supportive, because summer sun is what the roofs respond to.

why.A: No pupil is criticised. The passage says the reason is worth stating carefully, which is instruction rather than dismissal.
why.B: The shade result is reported as clear — half a degree, inside the scatter — and is used to make the argument.
why.C: Correct. The conclusion is rejected, and the closing lines explain why the mistake survives most available evidence.
why.D: The passage denies exactly this: summer is not what the roofs respond to, direct sun is.

reading.context: Which result is essential to the argument the passage makes?

choices.text: The pale roof ran about four degrees cooler in full sun.
The gap fell to half a degree when the roofs stood in shade.
The four-degree figure agreed with the published values.
The class had predicted the size of the difference in advance.

why.A: The full-sun result establishes that colour matters. On its own it is consistent with the pupil’s reading as well.
why.B: Correct. The collapse in shade is the observation the passage has to explain, and the explanation is the argument.
why.C: Agreement with published figures supports the method but adds nothing to the question about shade.
why.D: A correct prediction speaks to the class rather than to why the two roofs converge.

reading.context: The passage proceeds by:

choices.text: giving two results, rejecting a reading of them, and explaining why.
describing an experiment, listing its errors, and proposing a redesign.
stating a physical law and deriving two predictions from it.
comparing published figures with a class’s own measurements.

why.A: Correct. Sun and shade come first, the pupil’s conclusion is rejected, and the final paragraphs give the reason.
why.B: No errors are found in the procedure, and no redesign is suggested anywhere.
why.C: The explanation about absorption arrives after the measurements, as an account of them rather than a starting point.
why.D: The published figures appear in one clause, as a check on the first result rather than as the subject.

reading.context: The two trials described in the passage differed mainly in:

choices.text: the colours that the two model roofs were painted.
the number of temperature readings that were taken.
how much direct sunlight reached the model roofs.
the season of the year in which they were conducted.

why.A: The same pale and charcoal roofs are used both times; that is what makes the comparison possible.
why.B: Reading counts are never given, though the scatter of the readings is mentioned once.
why.C: Correct. The first trial was in full sun on the field, the second in the shade of the science block.
why.D: They were a week apart, which is the passage’s reason for ruling the season out as the cause.

reading.context: The phrase "the quantity it operates on has gone to nearly nothing" refers to the:

choices.text: temperature difference recorded beneath the two roofs.
quantity of paint applied to each of the model roofs.
amount of sunlight arriving at the roof surfaces.
range of scatter across the class’s repeated readings.

why.A: That difference is the outcome being explained, so it cannot also be what the effect operates on.
why.B: Paint thickness is never discussed. Colour is treated as a property, not as a quantity that varies.
why.C: Correct. The preceding sentence says colour changes how much striking sunlight is absorbed, and shade removes the striking sunlight.
why.D: Scatter describes measurement noise and is used to judge the half-degree, not as the thing colour acts on.

reading.context: Which statement best summarises Bardo’s approach to the banner?

choices.text: A visible repair keeps the banner’s history readable.
A committee overruled the conservator’s chosen method.
Two-century-old silk is too fragile to be repaired.
Recording damage matters more than treating it.

why.A: The lighter net is deliberately visible so a later visitor can tell the guild’s silk from Bardo’s work.
why.B: The committee expected a seamless mend and one member objected, but nothing says they overruled her.
why.C: The silk is discoloured and torn, yet Bardo repairs it successfully; fragility is not the passage’s claim.
why.D: She photographs the tear before treating it, but the photographs support the repair rather than replace it.

reading.context: According to the passage, Bardo spent her first week doing what?

choices.text: Stitching a new gold lion into the banner’s centre.
Examining, photographing, and testing the banner.
Training the guild committee in basic conservation.
Dyeing a net to match the silk around the tear.

why.A: The gold lion is described as part of the original stitching, not as something Bardo replaced.
why.B: She looked, photographed the tear from eight angles, and tested the dye before beginning any treatment.
why.C: The committee asks her when she will begin; she instructs no one and offers no training.
why.D: She does dye a net, but that belongs to the repair itself, which comes after the first week.

reading.context: The passage most strongly suggests that Bardo regards a repair as:

choices.text: a failure to be hidden as completely as possible.
a decision best left to the object’s owners.
a record that future viewers are meant to read.
a step that should be delayed for as long as it can.

why.A: A seamless repair is exactly what she declines; concealment is the thing that loses information.
why.B: The committee hired her and questioned her timing, but the method described is hers rather than theirs.
why.C: She calls the lighter net a sentence in the banner’s history, written to be read by someone later.
why.D: Her first week of study is preparation, not delay; she tells the committee she has already begun.

reading.context: As used in this passage, “documented” most nearly means:

choices.text: filed paperwork with the guild’s own committee.
proved that a claim about the silk was true.
described an event in careful written detail.
let a later observer see what had been done.

why.A: No forms or records are submitted to the committee; the documenting happens in the banner itself.
why.B: Nothing in the sentence is being proved or disputed; the issue is what a future viewer can see.
why.C: The everyday sense of writing something down is close, but Bardo’s record is stitched, not written.
why.D: A seamless mend would have documented nothing, because nobody later could tell the two silks apart.

reading.context: The primary function of the passage’s final sentence is to:

choices.text: restate her reasoning as an image of writing.
introduce a disagreement the passage leaves open.
correct the committee member’s word for the mend.
explain why the silk faded over two centuries.

why.A: Calling the net a sentence written plainly enough to be read turns her explanation into a figure.
why.B: The disagreement with the committee is raised earlier, and the final line settles rather than opens it.
why.C: She does not dispute the word the member used; the sentence builds on her reasoning instead.
why.D: Fading is mentioned in the opening description and has nothing to do with the closing image.

reading.context: The passage’s attitude toward the notebook is best described as:

choices.text: sceptical that so small a change mattered.
approving of a plain solution that worked.
impatient with the association’s slow start.
neutral about whether the shed should exist.

why.A: Nothing hedges the result; returns improved within a month and the passage treats that as real.
why.B: The passage credits the notebook with saving the shed and explains without irony why it worked.
why.C: The bad first year is reported plainly, without blame aimed at the association’s pace.
why.D: A neutral account would not say the notebook saved the shed, which is a judgement in its favour.

reading.context: Which detail best supports the claim that the shed’s problem was not security?

choices.text: A hedge trimmer vanished during the first year.
Forty households shared a single circular saw.
The fix was a notebook, and no lock was added.
The association considered selling what remained.

why.A: A missing trimmer is the problem being explained, not evidence about what the problem was.
why.B: Sharing one saw is the shed’s purpose and says nothing about why tools went missing.
why.C: The passage states directly that what saved the shed was not a lock but the open notebook.
why.D: Talk of selling shows how bad the first year was, not what the underlying cause turned out to be.

reading.context: Which describes the order in which the shed’s story is told?

choices.text: a list of rules, then the penalties behind them.
two sheds compared across the same time period.
one borrower’s story, widened to the whole town.
a failed year, then the change that reversed it.

why.A: The scheme has no penalties at all — no fines, no deposits — so no such list appears.
why.B: Only one shed is described; the comparison here is between kinds of borrower, not places.
why.C: Feyi proposes the scheme, but no single borrower is followed through the passage.
why.D: The first paragraph is the bad year; the rest introduces the notebook and reports the result.

reading.context: The passage contrasts a borrower who can see the next borrower with one who:

choices.text: answers to a rule rather than to a person.
pays a deposit before taking any tool out.
has no particular need for the tool at all.
lives too far from the shed to return it.

why.A: Feyi sets a borrower who keeps an appointment against one who merely answers to a rule.
why.B: Deposits are explicitly not taken, so they cannot be the other half of the contrast.
why.C: Need is never raised; the contrast is about what makes a borrower return something on time.
why.D: Distance plays no part in the passage’s account of why tools came back late.

reading.context: The statement that the shed “had become smaller” most nearly means that it had become:

choices.text: a building with less floor space than before.
a place where members recognised one another.
a collection holding fewer tools than at first.
a scheme open to fewer than forty households.

why.A: The shed’s dimensions never change; smaller describes the social distance inside it.
why.B: The sentence glosses itself: a room where forty households could see one another.
why.C: Tools did go missing, but the sentence is about how borrowers relate, not about inventory.
why.D: Membership stays at forty households throughout; nothing narrows who may take part.

reading.context: Which statement best captures what happens to the narrator during the journey?

choices.text: A familiar route is discovered to be dangerous.
A long habit is deliberately broken for once.
Irritation at a mistake gives way to attention.
An error is concealed from other passengers.

why.A: Nothing in the ride is unsafe; what changes is what the narrator notices, not any risk.
why.B: The wrong train is boarded by habit rather than by choice — the eyes-shut line makes that plain.
why.C: The narrator sits in embarrassment, begins looking out properly, and stops being annoyed.
why.D: Other passengers are never mentioned, and the embarrassment is private rather than hidden.

reading.context: How long does the narrator read before noticing that something is wrong?

choices.text: Nine minutes, the length of the first chapter.
The whole way to Colwick, without looking up.
Only a moment, before the doors had closed.
Eleven minutes, until a field looked wrong.

why.A: Nine is the number of years on this route, not the minutes spent reading.
why.B: Colwick is where the journey ends; the mistake is noticed long before that.
why.C: The train has left and the book is open before anything seems out of place.
why.D: It was eleven minutes before the narrator looked up and failed to recognise a field.

reading.context: The narrator’s remark about finding the platform with closed eyes mainly prepares the reader for:

choices.text: a habit strong enough to ignore a change.
a narrator who has come to dislike commuting.
a railway that hides its timetable changes.
a passenger travelling without any luggage.

why.A: Boarding by habit on the very morning the timetable changed is what puts the narrator on the wrong train.
why.B: Nine years of the same train suggests routine, but no dislike of the commute is expressed.
why.C: The timetable change is stated plainly; the passage never accuses the railway of concealing it.
why.D: Luggage is never mentioned and has no bearing on how the mistake happens.

reading.context: As used in this passage, “properly” most nearly means:

choices.text: in the manner the railway recommends.
with real attention instead of habit.
politely, without disturbing anyone else.
correctly, after checking the timetable.

why.A: No railway instruction is involved; the word describes the quality of the looking, not compliance.
why.B: The narrator has not looked out since the first week, so the word marks a return to real noticing.
why.C: Courtesy toward other passengers is not at issue anywhere in the paragraph.
why.D: Checking a timetable is what the narrator failed to do, and it happens before boarding.

reading.context: The half-finished whale mural functions in the passage chiefly to:

choices.text: show that the town neglects its own school.
hint that the train has travelled in a circle.
mark where the narrator’s mood begins to turn.
explain why the line runs behind the houses.

why.A: The mural is unfinished, which the passage reports without judging the school or the town.
why.B: The route is unfamiliar rather than circular; this is a different line, not a loop.
why.C: The last sentence places the change somewhere past the whale, making the mural the hinge.
why.D: The line’s position behind the houses is stated separately and is not caused by the mural.

reading.context: The passage’s closing remark about the northern boundary conveys a sense of:

choices.text: alarm at how much fruit had been lost.
doubt about the student’s measurements.
regret that the poplars were planted.
an answer that was available all along.

why.A: The passage never counts lost fruit or treats the other rows’ yield as a loss.
why.B: Reike’s figures are reported without qualification and drive the passage’s conclusion.
why.C: The poplars turn out to be the cause of the better rows, so there is nothing to regret.
why.D: The poplars had stood there for forty years; the line is about a plain fact overlooked.

reading.context: Which finding most directly rules out drainage as the cause of the difference?

choices.text: It varied by less than the instrument’s error.
The water table sat at the same depth throughout.
The trees came from one nursery in one spring.
Wind speed differed sharply between the rows.

why.A: Variation smaller than the measurement error is variation the block does not actually have.
why.B: A level water table is related evidence, but drainage is settled by the drainage figures.
why.C: Identical planting stock rules out the trees as a variable, not the ground they stand in.
why.D: The wind result supplies the real cause; it does not by itself eliminate the older one.

reading.context: Reike’s account moves from:

choices.text: a single season to a forty-year record.
an old assumption to a measured cause.
a farmer’s complaint to a policy change.
a general rule to one unusual exception.

why.A: Two seasons of logging appear, but the shape is explanation replacing assumption.
why.B: Better drainage is the unmeasured assumption; wind at blossom height is what the data give.
why.C: No complaint and no policy decision appear anywhere in the account.
why.D: Rows four and five are the case under study, not an exception to a rule stated earlier.

reading.context: Compared with rows nine and ten, rows four and five are:

choices.text: planted in noticeably richer soil.
watered on a more frequent schedule.
far better sheltered from the wind.
made up of younger, smaller trees.

why.A: Soil nitrogen varied by less than the instrument’s error across the whole block.
why.B: Every row receives the same water on the same schedule, which the passage states outright.
why.C: The poplars shelter rows four and five almost completely, while nine and ten stand in the open.
why.D: All the trees went in the same spring from the same nursery, so none of them is younger.

reading.context: In saying the orchard had been “running an experiment” without noticing, the passage suggests that:

choices.text: the growers deliberately withheld their results.
the orchard was designed by a research team.
the poplars were planted to test the bees.
a chance arrangement produced usable evidence.

why.A: Nobody in the passage knows there is a result, so no one could be holding one back.
why.B: The orchard is a working farm; Reike arrives decades later to measure what is already there.
why.C: The poplars went in during the 1970s for shelter, long before anyone thought of pollination.
why.D: A windbreak planted for its own reasons created two conditions side by side, as an experiment does.

reading.context: The bench episode chiefly demonstrates:

choices.text: how seating shapes what visitors notice.
why certain paintings are worth more.
how one curator rehung an entire gallery.
what makes a museum survey reliable.

why.A: Moving one bench changed which pictures visitors remembered, without changing any picture.
why.B: Value and price never come up; the survey asks what people remembered, not what anything is worth.
why.C: Voss explicitly moved no paintings — that is what makes the result meaningful.
why.D: The survey is the instrument that reveals the change, not the subject the passage examines.

reading.context: What did Voss change in 2011?

choices.text: The lighting above the long room’s door.
The bench’s position and its direction.
The order in which the paintings hung.
The wording used in the spring survey.

why.A: Lighting is never mentioned as part of the change or as an explanation of the result.
why.B: She moved it four metres and turned it ninety degrees, leaving everything else where it was.
why.C: The passage states that she did not move a single painting.
why.D: The survey runs every spring with the same question, which is why answers can be compared.

reading.context: Voss’s final remark implies that decisions affecting what visitors see are often made by:

choices.text: the artists whose work is on display.
visitors who choose their own route.
people with no curatorial role at all.
committees that approve each new display.

why.A: The artists’ choices end at the canvas; the passage is about where the canvas is met from.
why.B: Visitors are the people affected by the arrangement rather than the ones setting it.
why.C: She says most of those decisions are made by people who never think of themselves as curators.
why.D: No approval process appears, and the bench was moved by a single curator.

reading.context: As used in the final sentence, “rest” most nearly means:

choices.text: recover from an earlier effort.
depend on something for support.
remain unused for a long period.
settle and stay for a while.

why.A: Physical recovery is what the bench offers the body, but the phrase is about the eyes.
why.B: The sense of relying on something does not fit a sentence about where eyes land.
why.C: Nothing is described as idle or unused; the eyes are actively looking at one picture.
why.D: The sentence is about where a visitor’s gaze comes to a stop and stays for a few minutes.

reading.context: The sentence stating that Voss has been careful about her claims serves mainly to:

choices.text: narrow the conclusion the result can carry.
cast doubt on the survey’s yearly results.
credit the gallery’s staff for the change.
introduce a rival explanation for the data.

why.A: It sets up what follows: the bench did not improve the landscape, only what visitors looked at.
why.B: The survey’s findings are accepted throughout; what is limited is the interpretation.
why.C: No staff other than Voss is mentioned in connection with the change.
why.D: The sentence leads into her own explanation rather than setting an alternative against it.

reading.context: How does the passage regard the postmasters’ log?

choices.text: amused by the notebooks’ untidy handwriting.
respectful of what its consistency achieved.
doubtful that the readings can be trusted.
indifferent to which record researchers use.

why.A: The illegible hands are noted as a limitation, not as something the passage finds funny.
why.B: It calls an unbroken habit the rarer qualification, which is praise for exactly that steadiness.
why.C: The readings are called rough rather than untrustworthy, and the archive group builds on them.
why.D: The passage argues for one record over the other, which is the opposite of indifference.

reading.title: The Repaired Clock
reading.blurb: Original short passage for focused reading practice.
reading.text:
When Mira carried the station clock into the workshop, she set it down the way you set down something you have already decided about. The face was scratched — one long line running from the numeral four almost to the centre — and she had spent the walk deciding what colour to repaint it.

Her grandfather turned the case over and opened the back instead. For an hour he did nothing to the face at all. He cleaned the mechanism, oiled two pivots, and put a new suspension spring in place of one that had gone brittle. The clock began to tick. The scratch remained.

Mira said she could still fix that part. He asked her whether she knew what had made it. She did not. He told her that the keeper who had run the station before the line closed used to mark the face each time a service was added, and that the long line was the evening train, scored deeper than the others because he had been pleased about it.

She looked at the mark for a while after that. It had not become prettier. It had become legible. On the shelf at home it kept time badly and said something exactly, and she found she preferred that arrangement to the other one.
